(p-66) His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Yes (بَلى)﴾. Al-Farra' said: The meaning is, "Yes, he will certainly return (لَيَحُورَنَّ)." Then he resumed, and the Exalted said: ﴿Indeed, his Lord has been ever Seeing of him﴾. The exegetes (al-mufassirun) said: "Seeing of him in all his circumstances."

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿So I swear not﴾. Its explanation has already preceded.

As for "the twilight" (al-shafaq), Ibn Qutaybah said: There are two twilights: the red and the white. The red lasts from the setting of the sun until the time of the night prayer (ṣalāt al-ʿishāʾ), and then it disappears, while the white twilight remains until midnight.

The exegetes have six opinions regarding what is meant by "the twilight" here.

The first: it is the redness that remains on the horizon after the sun sets. Ibn (ʿUmar) narrated that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The twilight is the redness." This is the view of ʿUmar, his son, Ibn Masʿud, ʿUbadah, Abu Qatadah, Jabir ibn ʿAbd Allah, Ibn ʿAbbas, Abu Hurayrah, Anas, Ibn al-Musayyab, Ibn Jubayr, Tawus, Makhul, Malik, al-Awzaʿi, Abu Yusuf, al-Shafiʿi, Abu ʿUbayd, Ahmad, Ishaq, Ibn Qutaybah, and al-Zajjaj. Al-Farra' said: I heard some of the Arabs say, while wearing a dyed garment: "It is like the twilight," and it was red.

The second: it is the daytime.

The third: it is the sun. Both of these two opinions are narrated from Mujahid.

The fourth: it is what remains of the daytime. This was said by ʿIkrimah.

The fifth: it is the darkness that occurs after the whiteness has gone. This was said by Abu Jaʿfar Muhammad ibn ʿAli.

The sixth: it is the whiteness. This was said by ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAziz.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And by the night and what it gathers (wa mā wasaq)﴾. That is: and what it gathers and brings together. They cited the verse of poetry:

*Indeed we have she-camels, pure-bred, that gather together, if only they found a driver.*

(p-67) Abu ʿUbaydah said: "What it gathers (wa mā wasaq)" means whatever rises up, so that nothing is withheld from it. When the night covers the mountains, the trees, the seas, and the earth, and they all gather under it, then it has gathered them. Some of them said: The meaning of "what it gathers" is what gathers, from what had been dispersed during the day in its activities, to its resting place.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And by the moon when it becomes full (idhā ittasaq)﴾. Al-Farra' said: Its becoming full (ittisāquh) is its coming together and becoming complete on the thirteenth, fourteenth, up to the sixteenth night.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿You will surely embark (la-tarkabunna) from stage to stage (ṭabaqan ʿan ṭabaq)﴾. Ibn Kathir, Hamzah, and al-Kisa'i recited ﴿la-tarkabunna﴾ with a fatha on the *tā'* and the *bā'*, and there are two opinions regarding its meaning.

One of them: it is an address to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). Then, regarding its meaning, there are two views. One: "You will surely embark heaven after heaven," said by Ibn Masʿud, al-Shaʿbi, and Mujahid. The other: "You will surely embark state after state," said by Ibn ʿAbbas, who said: "He is your Prophet."

The second opinion: the reference is to the heaven. The meaning is that it changes in various kinds of alteration: at one time it is like molten metal (al-muhl), and at another time like oil (al-dihān). This is also narrated from Ibn Masʿud.

ʿAsim, Nafiʿ, Abu ʿAmr, and Ibn ʿAmir recited ﴿la-tarkabunna﴾ with a fatha on the *tā'* and a ḍamma on the *bā'*, and it is an address to all people. Its meaning is: you will surely embark state after state. Ibn Masʿud, Abu al-Jawza', and Abu al-Ashhab recited ﴿la-yarkabanna﴾ with a *yā'* and a fatha on the *bā'*. Abu al-Mutawakkil, Abu ʿImran, and Ibn Yaʿmar recited ﴿la-yarkabunna﴾ with a *yā'* and a ḍamma on the *bā'*. The word "ʿan" (عَنْ, "from") here has the sense of "after" (بَعْدَ). This is the view of the majority of exegetes and linguists, and they cited for al-Aqraʿ ibn Habis:

One: they are the hardships and terrors, then death, then resurrection, then the gathering (al-ʿarḍ), said by Ibn ʿAbbas.

The second: it is ease after hardship, and hardship after ease, wealth after poverty, and poverty after wealth, health after sickness, and sickness after health. [Said by al-Hasan.]

The third: it is the human being's condition of being a suckling infant, then weaned, then a young boy, then an old man. [Said by ʿIkrimah.]

The fourth: it is the change of the human being's state in the Hereafter after this world, so that the one who was lowly is raised up, and the one who was exalted is brought low. This is the view of Saʿid ibn Jubayr.

The fifth: it is following the ways of those who came before them of the earlier peoples. Said by Abu ʿUbayd.

Some of the wise used to say: Whoever is in one state today and another state tomorrow should know that his management is in the hands of Another.
